rows.subtype: Approach: naming the competing values [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl asked to skip a robotics camp to help at her family's shop writes down what family duty and her own ambition each mean to her, so the conflict is understood rather than only felt.

rows.subtype: Approach: listing options beyond either-or [Thinking]
rows.description: Instead of just yes or no, the student brainstorms half-days at the shop, a sibling covering some shifts, or joining a shorter robotics programme, widening the choices.

rows.subtype: Approach: sacrificing the dream silently [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student gives up the camp without a word to avoid conflict. The decision seems dutiful, but hidden resentment grows and the family never learns what was given up.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the compromise after a month [Revision]
rows.description: A month later the student and family assess whether the schedule works, adjusting shifts and confirming that each person's effort is seen, so the arrangement remains fair.

rows.subtype: Approach: breaking the move into a checklist by weeks [Action]
rows.description: A sales executive moving from Lucknow to Bengaluru lists tasks: notice period, house search, school for the child, packers, and address changes, with a date for each.

rows.subtype: Approach: visiting first to assess neighbourhoods [Action]
rows.description: He spends a weekend in the new city, checks commute times at peak hours, and visits three areas. The visit replaces online guesses with direct experience before signing a lease.

rows.subtype: Approach: underestimating settling costs and time [Pitfall]
rows.description: Assuming everything will be sorted in a week, a family arrives with little cash and no internet or gas connection. Deposits and setup costs cause stress in their first month.

rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting after the first month in the new city [Revision]
rows.description: Finding the commute exhausting, he moves to a flat closer to the office despite the lease penalty. He recognises that the first choice was made with limited information.

rows.subtype: Approach: reflecting before responding [Thinking]
rows.description: After a friend shares a secret with others, the student waits a night, writes down what hurt and what outcome is wanted, and realises the goal is to be heard and trusted again, not to win.

rows.subtype: Approach: win-win repair plan [Action]
rows.description: Both agree on a clear rule that private things stay private, the friend apologises to the affected person, and they plan a shared weekend activity to rebuild ease, so both needs are met.

rows.subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
rows.description: Hurt and angry, the student posts vague complaints in a shared chat. It draws sympathy for a moment but spreads the conflict, embarrasses the friend and makes an honest talk much harder.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing the first talk failed and trying a different way [Revision]
rows.description: When the face-to-face talk turns into shouting, the student sends a short calm message the next day suggesting a walk, showing that a change of setting and tone can reopen the discussion.

rows.subtype: Approach: separating positions from interests [Thinking]
rows.description: One co-founder wants to raise money now and the other wants to stay bootstrapped. Asking why reveals that one fears losing control and the other fears missing the market window.

rows.subtype: Approach: bringing in a trusted mentor as mediator [Action]
rows.description: When talks stall over equity, the founders ask a senior friend who has run a company to hear both sides. The mentor asks each to restate the other's view before proposing options.

rows.subtype: Approach: avoiding the conflict to keep peace [Pitfall]
rows.description: A founder stays silent about a partner's missed deadlines for months. Resentment builds and comes out in one angry message during a client call, harming both the work and trust.

rows.subtype: Approach: revising roles after a trial period [Revision]
rows.description: After a quarter, both admit the technical founder is weak at sales calls. They swap so the co-founder leads customers, and the technical founder focuses on delivery, and satisfaction rises.

rows.subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
rows.subtype: Approach: values-first clarity before the talk [Thinking]
rows.description: Before speaking to parents, a young adult writes what matters: finishing a degree, financial independence and choosing a partner freely, and what could be flexible, such as timing.

rows.subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
rows.subtype: Approach: empathy for the parents' worries [Thinking]
rows.description: The young adult thinks about why parents raise marriage, such as security and social expectations, and plans to acknowledge their care before stating a different view.

rows.subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
rows.subtype: Approach: angry outburst and ultimatum [Pitfall]
rows.description: Frustrated after repeated calls from relatives, the young adult shouts that they will never marry, and parents become more anxious and dig in, ending the conversation.

rows.subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
rows.subtype: Approach: continuing the conversation in small steps [Revision]
rows.description: After the first tense talk, the young adult sends a calm message, shares career news regularly, and returns to the topic later, letting trust grow slowly instead of winning at once.

rows.subtype: Approach: time-boxing a weekly schedule [Action]
rows.description: The student blocks two hours of study after school, one hour of football at five, and thirty minutes of gaming after homework is done, and pastes the grid above her desk.

rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising by urgent versus important [Thinking]
rows.description: Facing a test in three days and a district match on Saturday, the student separates what is due soon from what matters long term, and drops a lower-value gaming session while keeping sport.

rows.subtype: Approach: promising to cut screens completely [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student swears to delete all games and social apps. The all-or-nothing rule lasts four days, then a single slip is treated as total failure and the old habit returns at full strength.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing and loosening an unrealistic plan [Revision]
rows.description: After two weeks of missing targets, the student sees the schedule left no room for travel or festivals. He trims study blocks slightly, keeps sport fixed and allows one guilt-free screen evening.
